result:
The answer 1/3 holds up, though my upper-bound check is only a sketch and not a full proof.

**Construction.** Holes sit at cells (2a, 2b) in a 2m × 2m square. Two such holes are at least 2 apart in some coordinate, so their boundary vertex sets {2a, 2a+1} × {2b, 2b+1} are disjoint. Holes at a, b between 1 and m−1 keep their boundaries off the outer rectangle. Every cell with an odd coordinate is present and these cells form a connected set. The boundary cells with both coordinates even attach to odd neighbours. The count is (m−1)² holes among 3m² + 2m − 1 cells, so the ratio tends to 1/3. The construction is valid.

**Upper bound.** For single-cell holes, the argument is correct. The hole cells must be pairwise at king-distance at least 2, so each 2×2 block holds at most one hole. That gives k ≤ N/4 and hence k ≤ n/3.

The proposed solution asserts without proof that larger holes are never better. A hole with a anchor cell has a 2×2 block that can contain other cells of the same hole. The anchor blocks of different holes stay disjoint, but the 3-polyomino-cells-per-hole count then needs justification. I checked one alternative: horizontal domino holes at period 3 in x and 2 in y use 6 cells per hole, 4 of them polyomino cells. That gives a ratio of 1/4, which is worse than 1/3. Larger holes cost extra cells and share their surrounding cells no better, so 1/3 is very plausible as the true limit.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
